evidence: Plin. NH 9.5: tunc illīc ruunt turbinēs, tunc imbrēs
terms.comment: Latin names the rains themselves, as English speaks of “the rains”: Pliny’s imbrēs Aethiopiae aestīvī are the summer rains of the south that swell the Nile, and in the Indian Ocean the storms and rains come at the solstices. We have found no classical set phrase for the season as such; tempus imbrium would be a description of ours.

terms.gloss: winter, the rainy and stormy season
evidence: Hor. C. 1.4.1: solvitur ācris hiems grātā vice vēris et Favōnī
terms.comment: Lewis & Short gives “rainy season” among its senses: in the Mediterranean the rains fall in winter. Where the rainy season falls in the northern winter months, as in Indonesia, the word serves for it as it stands.
Egger’s phrase, in Morgan–Owens, after Pliny’s name for the monsoon wind: see “monsoon”.

phrases.latin: aut imbrēs Aethiopiae aestīvōs, īsdem etēsiīs nūbila illō ferentibus ē reliquō orbe
phrases.english: or the summer rains of Ethiopia, the same seasonal winds carrying the clouds there from the rest of the world

phrases.latin: Hieme hīc cotīdiē post merīdiem pluit.
phrases.english: In the rainy season it rains here every afternoon.

phrases.latin: Imbrēs jam adsunt: sine paenulā nē exīverīs.
phrases.english: The rains are here now: don’t go out without your raincoat.
